items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 2, provisions 2.4 and 2.7; Principle 7; Principle 9, provisions 9.1 to 9.2.1; Terminology table
items.quote: they shall undertake a due diligence assessment and should ensure that the provider is adhering to this Code of Practice
items.why: Source of the quotation. Voluntary: the terminology table says 'shall' indicates a requirement 'for the voluntary Code'. Provision 7.3 requires evaluations to be re-run on released models an organisation intends to use; 9.2.1 says independent security testers 'should' be used. The introduction says the Code builds on the NCSC guidelines of November 2023.

items.title: Implementation Guide for the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: Integrate security into the AI system’s design phase by conducting threat modelling
items.why: Worked examples of each provision for four kinds of system, from a chatbot to an open model. Commissioned by the department from a named external author and reviewed by department and NCSC officials; explanatory, not a requirement.

items.title: ETSI TS 104 223 V1.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.quote: should use independent security testers with
items.why: The international specification that carries the UK Code's provisions in the same words, so a supplier outside the UK can be asked to meet it. V1.1.1, April 2025, was the only version in the ETSI delivery folder on the date checked. A specification, not law.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development
items.quote: Security must be a core requirement, not just in the development phase, but throughout the life cycle of the system.
items.why: Sets the four stages: secure design, secure development, secure deployment, and secure operation and maintenance. Aimed primarily at providers of AI systems, including those building on external models or interfaces. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: Guidelines for secure AI system development: Secure development
items.quote: require suppliers to adhere to the same standards your own organisation applies to other software
items.why: The procurement test in one sentence. Also says to be ready to move to an alternative for critical systems if security criteria are not met.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 32: Security of processing
items.quote: a process for regularly testing, assessing and evaluating the effectiveness of technical and organisational measures for ensuring the security of the processing
items.why: The binding rule, and it is not specific to AI: controllers and processors must secure personal data to a level appropriate to the risk, having regard to the state of the art. Applies only where personal data is processed. Art. 32(3) amended by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 from 20 August 2025.

items.title: AI cyber security survey: main report
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: nearly half of respondents (47%) had no specific cyber security practices in place specifically for AI
items.why: Source of the figure. 350 telephone interviews, January to February 2024, with UK businesses using or planning to use AI; 239 were already using it. Unweighted, with larger businesses deliberately over-represented, so it describes the sample, not all UK businesses. Also found each AI technology was most often bought as external or ready-to-use software.

items.title: Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Introduction (modular approach to codes of practice); Principle A (risk management), action on suppliers
items.quote: such as the Software Security Code of Practice or the AI Cyber Security Code of Practice, should also follow the Cyber Governance Code of Practice
items.why: The board-level code: what directors should seek assurance on, including supply chain risk. Voluntary. It says organisations following the AI code should also follow this one.

items.title: LLM03:2025 Supply Chain
items.quote: in ML the risks also extend to third-party pre-trained models and data
items.why: Practitioner list of what to ask a supplier about: third-party models, training data, outdated components. Community consensus document, not a standard. No publication date is shown on the page.

items.title: Cyber Security and Resilience Bill (collection)
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.quote: The Bill has now completed its second reading and committee stage in the House of Commons.
items.why: Status of the Bill. First published 30 September 2024, last updated 18 November 2025. The page says the Bill was introduced on 12 November 2025 and will reform the Network and Information Systems Regulations 2018. Parliament's bills data on the date checked showed it in the House of Lords at report stage and not yet an Act. The page does not describe it as specific to AI.

items.title: UK GDPR, Article 28: Processor
items.quote: makes available to the controller all information necessary to demonstrate compliance with the obligations laid down in this Article
items.why: The binding rule on buying, where a supplier processes personal data for the organisation: use only processors giving sufficient guarantees of appropriate security, under a contract that gives the right to audit and inspect. This is the legal basis for the contractual obligations and audit rights the criterion's top level describes. Not specific to AI, and it applies only where the supplier is a processor of personal data.

items.title: ETSI EN 304 223 V2.1.1: Securing Artificial Intelligence (SAI); Baseline Cyber Security Requirements for AI Models and Systems
items.locator: Foreword, PDF p. 4 (status and adoption date); provisions 5.1.2-4 and 5.1.2-7, PDF pp. 10-11
items.quote: they shall undertake a due diligence assessment and should ensure that the provider is adhering to the present document
items.why: The UK Code's provisions as a European Standard, adopted 8 December 2025; it follows the April 2025 technical specification already on this list, and the NCSC now points to this version. The due diligence provision is unchanged. The foreword gives 30 September 2026 as the date for national publication or endorsement. A standard, not law: nothing obliges a UK organisation or its supplier to follow it unless a contract says so.

items.title: Machine learning principles: 2.1 Secure your supply chain
items.locator: Part 2: Secure development, principle 2.1, Goals and 'Verify any third-party inputs are from sources you trust'
items.quote: You understand that the risk of supply chain contamination heightens when you use models that don't have a transparent creation method.
items.why: What to check when a model, dataset or labelling service comes from outside: where it came from, whether it can be verified, and a bill of materials listing the third-party components. Gives a research example of a tampered model uploaded to a public model hub disguised as a popular one. Version 2.0, May 2024. Guidance, not a rule.

items.title: Software Security Code of Practice
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: 'Voluntary Software Security Code of Practice', theme 1 (principles 1.1 to 1.4) and theme 4
items.quote: Follow secure by design and secure by default principles throughout the development lifecycle of the software.
items.why: The government's baseline for any software sold to organisations, which is how most AI is bought: 14 principles, co-designed with the NCSC, with a named senior owner at the vendor who must gain assurance they are met. Gives a buyer a published standard to ask a supplier to attest to. Voluntary and not specific to AI; the page was last updated on 15 January 2026.

items.title: SS2/21 Outsourcing and third party risk management
items.locator: Chapter 8 'Access, audit, and information rights', para 8.3, PDF p. 31
items.quote: full access and unrestricted rights for audit and information
items.why: A UK regulator's stated expectation on contracts with suppliers: for material outsourcing, written agreements should give the firm, its auditors and the regulator full audit and information rights, and the firm should use them. A worked model of the criterion's top level. Applies to banks, building societies, insurers and designated investment firms only, and is not about AI. This is the version in force (effective 31 December 2024); a revised version published 18 March 2026 takes effect on 18 March 2027.

items.title: Government cyber resilience (HC 546, Session 2024-25)
items.locator: Summary, paras 15 and 19, PDF pp. 11 and 13
items.quote: This has provided better information than its previous approach of relying on departments' self-reported cyber resilience
items.why: An audit finding on the difference between assumed and verified security: when government moved from departments' own reports to assessment checked by independent reviewers, it found significant gaps across the 72 critical systems assessed, 58 of them checked by independent reviewers. Evidence for the step from the criterion's third level to its fourth. About central government IT in general, not AI and not procurement.

items.title: BadNets: Identifying Vulnerabilities in the Machine Learning Model Supply Chain
items.locator: Abstract on the arXiv record (version 2, 11 March 2019)
items.quote: we show that outsourced training introduces new security risks
items.why: The founding study of the bought-model risk: a model trained by someone else can pass the buyer's own tests yet misbehave on inputs the attacker chooses, and the hidden behaviour can survive retraining. Why a supplier's accuracy figures are not evidence of security. Cited from the authors' preprint on arXiv; only the abstract was read. Image classifiers from 2017, not language models.

items.title: An Empirical Study of Pre-Trained Model Reuse in the Hugging Face Deep Learning Model Registry
items.publisher: arXiv (Jiang, Synovic, Hyatt, Schorlemmer, Sethi, Lu, Thiruvathukal and Davis)
items.quote: Three challenges for PTM reuse are missing attributes, discrepancies between claimed and actual performance, and model risks.
items.why: Empirical study of how engineers pick up ready-made models from the largest public model hub: provenance is often missing and claimed performance does not always match what is measured. The arXiv record says it appeared in the proceedings of a peer-reviewed software engineering conference (ICSE 2023). Interviews with 12 practitioners plus measurements of one hub; only the abstract was read.

items.title: Guidelines on Securing AI Systems
items.locator: Section 3.3, guideline 2.1 'Secure the supply chain', PDF p. 11
items.quote: Ensure that suppliers adhere to security policies and internationally recognised standards, or that risks are otherwise appropriately managed.
items.why: International comparator. Singapore's national guidance takes the same line as the UK Code on bought components (training data, models, interfaces, software libraries) and suggests bills of materials and checks against vulnerability databases. Voluntary and non-prescriptive; no legal force in the UK.
